title: Trump Sidesteps SCOTUS With New Tariffs
author: Violet Jira
summary: The new tariffs range from 10% to 12.5%.
content: The Supreme Court previously blocked a key part of President Donald Trump's tariff policy. Jacquelyn Martin/AP The Trump administration unveiled a new slate of global tariffs on Thursday, again circumventing the Supreme Court after it struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariff policy earlier this year. Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, said Thursday that the administration would use Section of the Trade Act of to place new tariffs on 60 countries. The tariffs would range from 10% to 12.5% and target multiple allies. Canada, Mexico, and the United Kingdom would be subject to a 10% tariff. “The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” Greer said in a statement . The administration justified the tariffs by claiming that some of the countries have done too little to prevent the import of goods made with forced labor. Section allows the administration to place tariffs in response to unfair, unjustifiable, or discriminatory foreign trade practices. In February, the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to enact tariffs. The Trump administration then opted to use Section of the Trade Act of to levy a 10% global import tariff. But those tariffs cannot be in place for more than days and would expire on Friday without approval from Congress to extend them. The new tariffs would have no expiration date and were announced just days after Trump said he would place a 50% tariff on some Canadian goods . The renewed turbulence in the trade world comes just months before the midterm elections. “[Section] is really designed to be like an emergency power authority. I think they recognized they weren't going to keep this long term,” Andrew Siciliano, the global and U.S. head of trade and customs at KPMG, told NOTUS. “They were probably planning for six months to come up with a new mechanism to apply the tariffs.” The administration’s abrupt shifts in tariff policy have complicated the broader global trade environment. Siciliano described it as “extremely disruptive,” but that businesses are learning to anticipate and adjust.

title: It’s 9 A.M. Somewhere
author: Marissa Martinez
content: Shelves display bottles of tequila for sale at a Pennsylvania fine wine and spirits store, Saturday, Jan. 22, , in Harmony, Pa. Keith Srakocic/AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 23, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Half the states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration for trying to use federal emergency grant funding to control state election rules. The Senate rejected a war powers resolution in its first action since the ceasefire deal collapsed in a 47-49 split, with four Republican senators not voting. The House had passed a similar measure earlier in the day. Spotted: A House Rules Committee staffer carrying three bags of booze through security shortly after 9 a.m. Recess is upon us. THE ADMINISTRATION A Secret Service agent on JD Vance ’s detail is under investigation and potentially facing criminal charges after private information was apparently leaked to the media. The Pentagon will partner with UNC-Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech for a reworked educational program for service members after Secretary Pete Hegseth cut ties with several Ivy Leagues. Karoline Leavitt said the president’s patience with John Thune is “running out” during a press briefing today as multiple attempts to jam through the SAVE America Act continue to flounder in the upper chamber. “Maybe she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right? It’s 50 around here,” Thune told reporters in response. “Instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats.” THE COURTS The estranged MAGA lobbyists who were hired by rapper Boosie Badazz to secure a presidential pardon have inked a new deal to do the same for Rajendra Parikh , who pleaded guilty last year to conspiracy to commit bank fraud. The White House won’t intervene in the extradition process for “manosphere” influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate , who were arrested by U.S. Marshals in Florida last week. The Minnesota man who pleaded guilty to killing former state House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband was sentenced to life in prison today. THE HILL Mark Sanford , the former South Carolina governor, announced he’s running for the late Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat. The upper chamber is struggling to pass Graham’s last bill. The Senate HELP Committee abruptly canceled votes today for three Labor and Health and Human Services nominees — Erica Schwartz , Sean Kaufman and Keith Sonderling — due to attendance issues. Votes have been pushed to next week. WHERE’S THE CORSAGE? Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

title: Vance Secret Service Agent Investigated After Alleged Media Leak
author: Jenna Monnin, Raymond Fernández
summary: The unidentified agent is facing “an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry,” according to the agency.
content: The Secret Services is investigating leaks to the news media after MS NOW reported Vice President JD Vance’s security detail was “fed up” with Vance’s burdensome travel. ANTHONY BEHAR/Sipa USA via AP A Secret Service agent on Vice President JD Vance’s detail is under investigation and faces potential criminal charges after private information was apparently leaked to the media. The agent, who was not identified, “is the subject of an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry, involving allegations of compromising operational and information security,” Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi told NOTUS in a statement. MS NOW reported last week that Vance’s security team was “fed up” with the vice president's personal travel schedule and said some agents considered their assignments to be inappropriate and burdensome. The story included details about Vance’s schedule that were not publicly known, and the Secret Service agent who is under investigation is accused of being a source for the article, according to CNN , which first reported the probe. The Secret Service did not release any additional information about the matter. “One principle is unequivocal: any conduct that potentially threatens the safety of a protectee will not be tolerated,” Guglielmi said. The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. President Donald Trump’s administration has cracked down on federal officials’ communications with the news media in an effort to prevent leaks of government information. The Office of Personnel Management proposed a new rule in May to apply sweeping nondisclosure agreements across the federal workforce. Government employees within the Defense Department and other national security-focused agencies were already subject to the agreements. The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to four New York Times reporters over their reporting on security concerns regarding the new aircraft being used as Air Force One. The Qatari government gifted the Boeing -8 to the U.S. government in May , and it was retrofitted to serve as the presidential aircraft.

title: The Unknowns
author: Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: A U.S. Army carry team moves a transfer case containing the remains of Staff Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton of Fayetteville, N.C., into a transfer vehicle Wednesday, July 22, , at Dover Air Force Base, Del. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Today’s notice: Trump threatens Iran’s civil infrastructure — again. The House and Senate prepare for war powers votes. A fight brews at the DNC over which state goes first. Congress earns its paycheck. Darline Graham faces an “unknown” problem. And: state election officials sound the alarm. THE LATEST The next stage: “I don’t know what the objectives are, so it’s kind of hard to measure what success is,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic yesterday after attending the return of four fallen U.S. service members at Dover Air Force Base. “I know what success isn’t — going to Dover like I did today and seeing the service members coming back.” The term “forever war” has been thrust back into the zeitgeist, punctuated on Wednesday when U.S. Central Command launched the 12th consecutive day of airstrikes hours after Donald Trump attended his third dignified transfer since the Iran war began. He later called it the “toughest thing” he has to do as president. Bridges and power plants. Those are the next targets near Tehran, according to Trump, who threatened to train the U.S.’s military might on a new civilian infrastructure target in retaliation for every boat Iran strikes in the Strait of Hormuz. While the president has made similar claims before (and then backed down), these new claims carry more heft as the war escalates. The rhetoric is also escalating. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , the speaker of Iran’s parliament, wrote on X , “In a region where we do not sell oil, no one will sell oil. If our security is not ensured, no infrastructure will be safe, and the security of the strait is in the absence of American forces.” Another front: Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks against two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, just days after announcing a blockade against Saudi Arabia, The Guardian reports . The House and Senate are expected to vote — yet again — this morning on a war powers measure to curtail the president’s war as his language ratchets up. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia), who has opposed previous resolutions restricting war powers, told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva that civilian targets should be off the table: “I don’t want anything to do with blowing up the bridge. And when you blow up the bridge, you’re going to have civilian casualties for sure. Nobody wants that. Nobody in the world wants that, but what are you going to do?” Open tabs: The Next Big Tests for the Left: Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota (NYT); OpenAI blamed a hacking event on its AI models going rogue (AP); U.S signs nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that gives it path to enriching fuel (WaPo); Maine Democrat Troy Jackson has raised $1M for his Senate bid so far . (Politico) From the campaign trail Fight Club, DNC edition: Democrats are preparing for battle as a handful of states jockey to lead off the presidential nominating calendar for . That lobbying campaign is being waged through phone calls and media attention, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports . “We’re first, and we maintain that,” Christale Spain , the chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party, said on journalist Roland Martin ’s YouTube show Monday. South Carolina, where voting Democrats are majority Black, is locked in a tense fight to go first with Nevada, with its strong Latino constituency. The Rules and Bylaws Committee meets Friday to make its recommendation. “It’s going to be a bloodbath,” said one of the members, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Most states represented have at least one or two members on the committee, and I think they’re all going to fight to the death for this.” First on NOTUS: NRDC’s midterm play. The political spending arm of the Natural Resources Defense Council plans to spend more than $6 million this cycle on ads aimed at flexing environmental voter muscle. While the topic has been ignored of late in favor of fights over who can lower energy prices the fastest by any means necessary, the NRDC’s new ads try to connect those dots with data-center politics. The first spots are going up in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District against Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan , a top target for Democrats. The ads have a podcast bro-y energy — pretty different from the earnest “In the Arms of an Angel”-style environmental appeals of old. One spot focuses on stock trading , specifically on Bresnahan’s purchase of stock in a data-center supplier. From the Hill A day in the life: The House finally did what few believed possible just a few weeks ago: pass some big-ticket legislation. House Republicans banded together with a - vote to ram through the third reconciliation package this term, this one coming in at $95 billion, NOTUS’ Stephen Neukam reports . Democrats banded together to oppose the funding for the war in Iran, farm aid and grants incentivizing states to adopt restrictive voter-ID laws on their own. The House also passed (with some Democratic support) the $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act to muscle through Trump’s plans for the Pentagon and the Stop Insider Trading Act , which would curb members of Congress and their families from purchasing individually traded stocks. Now, it’s the Senate’s turn, but don’t hold your breath for all of it: the chamber is historically not in a rush. Speaking of that side of the Capitol, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) is officially in the race to succeed her late brother, Lindsey Graham, but the question still remains: what does she believe? NOTUS’ Igor Bobic, Al Weaver and Oriana González report on the quandary facing Republicans who don’t personally know Graham or where she stands, despite wholeheartedly endorsing her. “These are people with legislative records that they can point to, that are proven to say, ‘Hey, prices are up, we can bring prices down if we do X, Y and Z. Here’s what I’ve done in the past,’” CJ Westfall , chair of the Dorchester County Republican Party, told NOTUS. Darline Graham is “somebody that’s unproven and just has the stamp of approval by the president. I don’t think that’s the end-all, be-all for South Carolina.” NOTUS PERSPECTIVES A savvy social-media campaign — dubbed Nixonmaxxing — has made Richard Nixon cool again. Today at NOTUS Perspectives, Matt K. Lewis writes about why this is happening now and why it’s a good thing . NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Local news: House Committee Advances Bill Limiting D.C.’s Ability to Raise Taxes , by Martin Austermuhle In his NOTUS debut: You Have Dining Questions. Tom Sietsema Has Answers. Sports desk: Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp , by Martenzie Johnson NEW ON NOTUS Trump says he wants election security up, but some election officials are questioning why the federal government is failing to help protect states from possible cyberattacks ahead of the midterms, NOTUS’ Samuel Larreal reports . “The federal government knows that there are nation-state actors desperately trying to come after us and cause chaos in our elections, yet, they are reducing resources,” Steve Hobbs , Washington state’s Democratic secretary of state, told Sam. “We’re doing everything we can to try to protect ourselves with far less resources than we did before.” More: Soldier Shot Near White House Files Claim Against the Secret Service , by Jenna Monnin Trump Offered Gold Star Family a Ride on His New Air Force One , by Torrie Herrington Second WHCA Dinner Isn’t a Security ‘Redo’ for the Secret Service, Officials Say , by Derek Hawkins Software Vendor Denies Responsibility for New Jersey Voter-Registration Error , by Angie Orellana Hernandez NOT US Trump administration weighing military options in Mali, officials say , by John Hudson and Rachel Chason for The Washington Post People are watching the Reflecting Pool like reality TV. What does that say about us? title: Second WHCA Dinner Isn't a Security 'Redo' for the Secret Service, Officials Say
author: Derek Hawkins
summary: Friday’s media dinner was rescheduled after an attack cut the original event short.
content: Secret Service officials said they viewed the thwarted attack on the April dinner as a success. Secret Service officials on Wednesday voiced confidence in their security plan for President Donald Trump's visit Friday to the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, which was rescheduled after a gunman tried to attack the original event in April. In a rare briefing with reporters at the Secret Service headquarters, Director Sean Curran said officials had sent an advance team of agents to secure the event at the Waldorf Astoria and that they were taking standard steps to prepare. “We do expect bad people to show up. It’s just the reality of where we are,” Curran said, noting that the dinner was taking place amid a surge in threats against Trump and other protectees. “But we’re treating it no different than any other site that the president goes to.” Service officials did not provide specifics on their security plans for the event, which the White House Correspondents’ Association said last month would involve “significantly enhanced safety measures and new access procedures.” Officials said they viewed the thwarted attack on the April dinner as a success. But they emphasized that they didn’t see the rescheduled event as a reprise of security from the first. “We examine every single site and we change things and get better every single time,” Deputy Director Matthew Quinn said. “We’re not looking at this as a redo of a dinner. We’re looking at this as a presidential site with Cabinet members and other protectees there, just like every other site we do everywhere we go.” The original dinner, held April 25 at the Washington Hilton, was cut short after an armed man charged through a security checkpoint, firing his weapon and injuring a Secret Service officer before law-enforcement personnel stopped him. Trump and other officials were evacuated while many of the attendees took shelter behind tables and chairs. The suspect, Cole Tomas Allen, pleaded not guilty in May to charges of attempting to assassinate Trump and weapons violations. The Secret Service scrutiny over its security arrangements at the event, with some lawmakers questioning whether the security perimeter was sufficiently large and raising concerns about how Allen managed to book a room in the hotel. Curran briefed lawmakers privately in the days that followed, but Congress did not hold hearings on the attack. Speaking with reporters Wednesday, Curran defended the service’s handling of security at the dinner, saying the roughly -yard buffer from the magnetometer checkpoint to the podium was adequate. “How we set up that perimeter and where we ended it is where we felt comfortable, with our special teams, as to where we needed to put it,” Curran said. “We do expect things to happen at the magnetometers, unfortunately. But that’s why they are there. And that’s where it happened, and that’s where it ended. So it did work — the system worked.” Trump is expected to speak at the rescheduled dinner, which will host fewer attendees than the original. Trump previously owned and operated the Waldorf Astoria building as the Trump International Hotel before his company sold the lease in . Service officials said that, overall, threats against protectees were running higher than at any point in recent memory. They said the agency’s protective intelligence investigations are up 40% over last year. The increase has strained agents, officers and other staffers, many of whom already work long overtime hours, according to current and former officials. The shooting at the dinner in April was one of three shootings near the White House in the span of about a month that the Secret Service responded to — the most in recent history for the agency in such a short span. In May, service personnel shot a man who allegedly fired a gun at officers near Vice President JD Vance’s motorcade, and in a separate incident fatally shot a man who opened fire near the White House. Last month, the Secret Service and FBI said they disrupted a plot to use drones, explosives and snipers to kill politicians and other attendees at the UFC fight held on the White House lawn. At least eight people have been arrested and charged in connection with the alleged plot. The rescheduled correspondents’ dinner is part of a historically packed schedule of protective events the Secret Service has managed this summer that has included the July 4 fireworks celebration and other festivities around America’s 250th anniversary.

title: Trump Offered Gold Star Family a Ride on His New Air Force One
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: The family of the late Lt. Tyler Feehan rode with the president from Dover Air Force Base to a rally in Georgia.
content: Following the dignified transfer ceremony, President Donald Trump said he spoke with Lt. Tyler Feehan’s family and discovered that they were from Georgia — which prompted him to offer them a ride on his new jet and an opportunity to see his rally. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo President Donald Trump said he offered to give Gold Star family members a ride on his newly outfitted Air Force One Wednesday following a dignified transfer ceremony to honor fallen service members. He revealed the gesture at a campaign rally in Georgia, where he appeared with Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and Rep. Mike Collins, who is running for Senate. The family of Lt. Tyler Feehan, 25, appears to have taken him up on the offer. “I said, ‘So if you want, I’ll give you a ride on Air Force One. And they said, ‘Wow,’” Trump recalled during his remarks, adding of the plane: “It’s quite nice, I must say.” Trump also thanked Feehan’s family by name, saying that he was impressed by the young soldier’s sterling record. Feehan died in an Iranian attack on his base in Jordan last weekend. “To Sherry and Stephen and David, we will carry Tyler’s memory in our hearts forever, and I just want to thank you. It’s an honor to have you here today,” the president said, gesturing to the family. Also at the rally, Trump said attending the dignified transfer is the “toughest thing” he has done as president. Dignified Transfers take place at the Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, where U.S. service member's remains are transferred from an arriving aircraft to a transport vehicle, ensuring fallen troops are honored and that their bodies are handled with dignity. On Wednesday, the remains of four soldiers killed in the Iran war were brought back to American soil and honored. Those soldiers were Feehan; Pvt. Isabella Gonzalez, 19; Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30; and Sgt. Angel Rampersad, 28. Following the ceremony, Trump said he spoke with Feehan’s family and discovered that they were from Georgia — which prompted him to offer them a ride on his new jet and an opportunity to see his rally. The new Air Force One that Trump has been using for domestic flights — including Wednesday’s trip — was gifted to him from Qatar, and is set to be donated to Trump’s presidential library after he leaves office. Renovations to the luxury jet, including many security upgrades, cost approximately $ million in taxpayer funds. The jet is intended as a “bridge” between the aging Boeing jets used by previous presidents and two new aircrafts currently under construction. Those jets are years behind schedule and are due to be delivered in at the earliest. Trump took the upgraded Air Force One on its maiden voyage earlier this month on a trip to Turkey to attend a NATO summit, but did not ride the plane back to the U.S . due to widely reported security concerns. News stories outlining the aircraft’s security vulnerabilities led the Justice Department to serve a series of highly unusual subpoenas to New York Times reporters and their relatives in an attempt to unmask the confidential sources who spoke with the newspaper. One reporter’s mother was even targeted by the administration, according to the Times.

title: Soldier Shot Near White House Files Claim Against the Secret Service
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: Benjamin Del Real Jr.’s attorney said “it's clear as day” that the U.S. Secret Service shot his client.
content: Benjamin Del Real Jr.’s lawyers say they have a source who says a Secret Service agent shot their client during a gunfight with a suspect in May near the White House when Del Real was visiting Washington with his father. Alex Brandon/AP Benjamin Del Real Jr., a 25-year-old bystander who was injured during a Secret Service shootout with a suspect in May near the White House, has filed a personal-injury claim against the agency, alleging a Secret Service agent was actually the one who shot him. “We have a very reliable and confidential source that tells us — who saw the CCTV footage of this incident — who says in no uncertain terms that the Secret Service shot Ben,” Joseph Murphy, Del Real’s attorney, said. “It's clear as day.” Del Real and his father were visiting Washington on May 23 when the suspect, Nasire Best, opened fire on a security checkpoint near the intersection of 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW. Del Real, who is an active-duty U.S. Army soldier from Kansas, was hit by a bullet during the incident. During the news conference announcing the lawsuit, Murphy said that the Del Real family was standing about 20 yards away from the suspected gunman, telling reporters that meant the Secret Service should have been “more surgical in their taking down of the shooter.” Del Real’s attorneys have attempted to negotiate with the Secret Service, Murphy said, but they have not “gotten any real, definitive or substantive answers at all in terms of what occurred.” Del Real is filing a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which is the first step toward suing the federal government. “It's part of the reason why we're frustrated here, and we're seeking more answers,” Murphy told reporters. “We have given them two months. I think we've been reasonable.” Murphy acknowledged that the U.S. Secret Service is a “highly trained and highly effective organization,” but said agents “fell well short of their training” when Del Real was shot. The Secret Service referred questions about the claim to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Del Real was shot in the abdomen and tore his ACL during the incident, his lawyers said. Emergency services rushed Del Real to George Washington University Hospital to undergo emergency surgery where doctors removed parts of his colon and part of his small intestine. The soldier has had two surgeries since the shooting and has had to recover from an infection during his medical treatment. “I enlisted a year and a half ago, and it's been one of the greatest journeys that I've taken thus far in my life,” Del Real told reporters when asked about returning to his role in the U.S. Army. “I am concerned with the ability to be able to perform the job that I signed up to do at this time.”

title: Mamdani Says He Can’t Arrest Netanyahu if He Comes to New York
author: Manuela Silva
summary: The New York City mayor posted a two-minute video explaining that he does not have the authority to arrest the Israeli Prime Minister if he comes to New York City.
content: During his mayoral campaign, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani pledged to order the New York Police Department to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he were to come to New York City. NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he would not arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he comes to New York City, a pledge he made while campaigning for mayor last year. Netanyahu is expected to visit New York City in September for the annual United Nations General Assembly. Mamdani told The New York Times last week that he was “in active conversation” with the city’s law department over the matter, but said on Tuesday that he does not have the legal authority to enforce the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant out for Netanyahu. President Donald Trump responded to the mayor’s earlier comments in a Monday Truth Social post, saying the prime minister would not be arrested “in any way, shape or form” in the U.S. During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani pledged to order the New York Police Department to arrest Netanyahu if he were to come to New York City. He reaffirmed his desire to do so on Tuesday in a two-minute video , calling the prime minister the “architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people.” “My administration has reviewed every avenue available under applicable law to determine whether New York City could execute the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant if Benjamin Netanyahu came here,” Mamdani said. “It is clear we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.” He instead turned the onus to arrest Netanyahu onto the federal government, which is unlikely to do so: “I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant.” The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November , accusing them of crimes against humanity including murder, starvation, persecution, and attacks on Gazans.

title: Iran War Has Cost the U.S. Nearly $38 Billion
author: Joe Gould, Hamed Ahmadi
summary: In a funding request, Hegseth revealed the Pentagon has blown past its recent cost estimate for the conflict.
content: Democrats pressed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on why the Pentagon needed another $67 billion from Congress when it still has $75 billion in unobligated money from last year’s Republican package. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo The Pentagon expects the war with Iran to cost $37.5 billion through the end of September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators Tuesday — $8.5 billion over what the Trump administration estimated in May — as renewed fighting threatens to drive the price still higher. The disclosure came during a combative Senate Appropriations Committee hearing that exposed the political challenge facing the administration as it seeks nearly $88 billion in emergency funding. Democrats demanded an endgame and an accounting of the portion of the request that has little link to Iran, while Republicans argued Congress must pay the military’s bills and rebuild depleted munitions stock. Hegseth said the $37.5 billion figure includes what the Pentagon has already racked up in war costs, as well as anticipated military personnel, operations and maintenance expenses through Sept. 30. Experts last month estimated the war’s cost to be roughly $40 billion , before the ceasefire collapsed and daily strikes resumed. Democrats also questioned why the Pentagon needed another $67 billion from Congress when it still has $75 billion in unobligated money from last year’s Republican package. Hegseth said those funds were already intended for longer-term priorities such as the Golden Dome, shipbuilding, hypersonic weapons and expanded munitions production — and that “95%” of the $ billion Congress granted the Pentagon last year would be allocated by September. “That’s news to me,” said Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense. The hearing marked the most extensive public remarks from Hegseth and Dan Caine, the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, following the ceasefire’s collapse. The U.S. military announced the deaths of three service members last weekend, bringing the U.S. death toll to 17 since the conflict began. The Trump administration submitted an $87.6 billion supplemental spending request that includes $32.7 billion in Iran war costs, another $39.2 billion in nonwar national security activities and $15.6 billion in unrelated activities, including relief for farm aid and other domestic programs. The administration’s effort to combine the war money with politically popular domestic relief could complicate Democrats’ approach to spending negotiations. During the hearing, lawmakers from both parties highlighted financial strains on farmers and ongoing disaster-recovery needs in states including North Carolina and California. Republicans, led by Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), largely rallied behind the request. Collins argued that despite senators’ disagreements over the decision to go to war with Iran, Congress still has a responsibility to restore military readiness. “Our men and women in uniform do not decide our nation’s military strategy,” she said. “Congress has a responsibility to ensure that they have the tools, the training, and the support that they need to accomplish their missions.” Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the committee’s top Democrat, said much of the administration’s $88 billion request had little to do with the war — citing its inclusion of money for National Guard deployments in Washington, D.C., Army operations at the southern border, strikes against boats in the Caribbean and the munitions already requested through the administration’s budget. “My point is that a lot of this request does not feel like an emergency,” Murray said. Multiple Democrats challenged Hegseth to square the Trump administration’s assertions that Iran’s military had been severely degraded given its subsequent control of the Strait of Hormuz and continued strikes on U.S. and allied targets. In one of the hearing’s most heated exchanges, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) took aim at Trump’s claims last year that Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities had been destroyed. “Was it ‘obliterated’ or wasn’t it?” Gillibrand asked. “Why are there missiles left to hit Jordan and result in the loss of life of our brave men and women?” Hegseth pushed back. “The nuclear sites under Midnight Hammer were obliterated, but Iranians foolishly continued to attempt to pursue nuclear capabilities,” he said. “As we stated from the beginning, the Iranian defense industrial base is effectively gone, but they do have underground facilities because they're the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism, and they've spent 47 years trying to hide their missiles under mountains.” After Trump vowed the U.S. will soon bomb Iran’s underground Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site, Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) pressed for “straight answers” on whether the U.S. could destroy the country’s deeply buried nuclear facilities. But Hegseth didn’t go into detail. “A lot of our capabilities are classified,” he said. “But if anybody in the world can reach anything on God’s green earth, it’s the United States military.” Other Democrats questioned the prewar planning. Sen. Jack Reed (D-Rhode Island) argued that Hegseth had failed to prepare Trump for the risk that Iran would disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, drive up oil prices and continue striking U.S. forces. “Of course, the Strait of Hormuz was front and center in every single aspect of that,” Hegseth said, adding that Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping had been part of the military planning. Reed also asked Caine whether airstrikes alone could deter and defeat Iran, and he wanted to know whether the administration was considering a ground war. Caine declined to discuss possible troop deployments.

title: Trump Lifts the Ban on Direct U.S. Flights to Lebanon
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: U.S. carriers were barred from flying to the country after the TWA hijacking in .
content: President Donald Trump is jettisoning a ban on direct U.S. flights to Lebanon, a prohibition dating to the TWA hijacking in . Mark Schiefelbein/AP President Donald Trump reversed a decades-old ban Tuesday on U.S. carriers flying to Lebanon after telling the country’s leader in an Oval Office visit that it had been badly treated. “I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all U.S. airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Hopefully, other Countries will do the same. Enjoy!” Direct U.S. flights to Lebanon have been banned since after a militant group linked to Hezbollah hijacked a Trans World Airlines flight traveling from Athens to Rome. The hijackers detoured the TWA flight to Beirut, held it for 17 days and murdered U.S. Navy diver Robert Stethem. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun’s visit to Washington marked the first time a Lebanese head of state has visited the White House in nearly two decades. During the bilateral meeting in the Oval Office, Trump defended Lebanon and noted that he had a “very good” relationship with Aoun. “It's been a very badly treated place and country, and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with respect that it deserves,” Trump said of Lebanon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Aoun this past weekend to discuss the “trilateral framework” between the U.S., Lebanon and Israel. Israeli forces still remain in parts of southern Lebanon — though Israel committed to a phased withdrawal of its troops from the region as part of the framework established on June 26. “The United States remains committed to supporting this effort and Lebanon’s efforts to deliver security, peace and a better future for the Lebanese people,” Rubio wrote on X. Trump’s move overturns a “ Presidential Determination ” issued by President Ronald Reagan following the TWA hijacking that barred U.S. carriers from flying directly to Lebanon. In , President Bill Clinton eased the restrictions and allowed U.S. airlines to sell tickets through non-U.S. carriers to all passengers through interline agreements — though direct U.S. flights to Lebanon remained strictly prohibited.

title: U.S. Soldier Killed in Iraq Identified as North Carolina Father of Two
author: Raymond Fernández
summary: The 30-year-old was killed in an explosion while helping dispose of a downed Iranian drone in Iraq, officials said.
content: Swinton is the third U.S. service member killed in connection with the conflict over the past week. Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA via AP An active-duty Army soldier who was killed in an explosion while helping dispose of a downed Iranian drone in Iraq has been identified as the 17th U.S. military fatality tied to the conflict with Iran. The Department of Defense on Tuesday identified the soldier as 30-year-old Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton of Fayetteville, North Carolina. Swinton died Sunday at Erbil Air Base during a “controlled detonation of a downed one-way unmanned aerial system.” Swinton is the third U.S. service member killed in connection with the conflict over the past week. "USASMDC is saddened by the loss of Sgt. Swinton, whose death occurred during an operation to safeguard fellow Soldiers,” Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said in a statement to NOTUS. “His service will not be forgotten, and his sacrifice is not in vain. We will support Sgt. Swinton's family and his unit during this difficult period. His loss will inspire his fellow Soldiers to continue the mission,” Rafferty said. Swinton is survived by his wife and two children — a 4-year-old daughter and a 6-year-old son — according to his mother, Christel Swinton Andujar, who spoke with local news station WRAL. “His wife, Mia, and two beautiful children, were the center of his world. Every decision he made and every sacrifice he endured was with them in his heart. His love for them was unconditional, selfless, and unwavering," Swinton Andujar said. “I didn’t think this would be the last time I ever saw you. I have no words,” Mia Gonzalez-Swinton, the soldier’s wife, said in a Facebook post on Sunday. “I was informed this morning that my husband, Michael, was killed while serving in Iraq. I’m navigating how to process this so please bear with me,” she . According to the Army, Swinton earned multiple military decorations during his service, including the Army Commendation Medal, Army Achievement Medal, Army Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary Medal, Army Service Ribbon and the Combat Action Badge. “Sgt. Swinton was an experienced noncommissioned officer who took great pride in his work and the people around him,” Brig. Gen. John L. Dawber, commanding general of the 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command, said in a statement. “He answered the call to duty with courage, honor, and selfless dedication.” Swinton’s death follows the killing of two other U.S. service members over the weekend in an Iranian attack on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. Those victims were identified Monday as U.S. Army Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, a 19-year-old from Texas, and 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, a 25-year-old from Hawaii.

title: Escalation and Exhaustion
author: Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: Aircraft on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln that are operating in support of the war in Iran, on Tuesday, March 3, . U.S. Navy via AP Today’s notice: Congress grapples with the escalating Iran war. Hakeem Jeffries gets a DSA-shaped lifeline. Primary day in Arizona. A full legislative plate for House Republicans. And: Trump brings back (a version of) the tariffs. THE LATEST Fresh attacks: “It looked like things were tapering off, and now things look like they’re heating up,” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) told NOTUS as the Iran war inches closer to the five-month mark. With 17 service members confirmed killed in action and a hundred more injured since early July, there’s growing anxiety on Capitol Hill over the intensifying hostilities and the lack of justification for them. The U.S. launched a new round of airstrikes yesterday, the 10th consecutive day of the assault. The Houthis in Yemen declared a “maritime blockade” against Saudi Arabia, blocking off another key waterway and potentially opening up a new front in the war. Several lawmakers told NOTUS’ Hamed Ahmadi, Al Weaver and Igor Bobic that Congress should no longer remain on the sidelines and that the White House needs to explain where the conflict is headed (blink if this sounds familiar!). House Republicans will have a chance to ask Donald Trump about the escalations directly today, when he hosts some in the Oval Office at 5 p.m. And new details could come from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chair of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine when they get grilled by senators about the nearly $70 billion supplemental request for war funding. Expect some tough questions from both sides of the aisle. “The president is threatening escalation and war crimes, and suggesting this could be another forever war,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington) is expected to say, according to excerpts released this morning. Meanwhile, the president’s allies say Iran escalated first. “I’m not nervous that it is expanding,” House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (R-Florida) told Manuela. He said he thinks the daily bombings “will be the status quo” going forward. Stockpile shortcomings: It would take three and a half to six years to restock America’s interceptors and a number of other missiles to the point the Pentagon could juggle a major war and a smaller conflict — and that’s if Congress appropriated every dollar needed to replace them. That’s according to a new report out this morning by the pro-Israel Jewish Institute for National Security of America, NOTUS’ Joe Gould picked up. Open tabs: Democrat set to replace Platner in Maine led state Senate with a temper (WaPo); U.S. Sought Phone Records of Times Journalists and Their Relatives (NYT); Trump, Pushing Back on Mamdani, Says Netanyahu Won’t Be Arrested if He Comes to U.S. (WSJ); Chuck Edwards gifted pink and blue handguns to young female staffers (Axios) From the campaign trail The progressive push and pull: Congressional candidate Brad Lander (D-New York) says he’ll support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker if Democrats take back the House, even as he and other über-progressives run as insurgents against the status quo, NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz reports . “I look forward to voting for Hakeem to be the speaker of the House,” Lander told Daniella. “At the same time, I want a party and party leadership that can listen to the passion and anger that voters feel and be responsive to it, and that means showing people much more clearly than leadership have so far what we’re fighting for.” It’s part of the tug-of-war growing between DSA-aligned candidates challenging the establishment and the party’s center of political gravity. And that contest is playing out mostly in Jeffries’ backyard. It’s primary day in Arizona, and all eyes are on the Democratic contest in the 1st Congressional District, an open-seat toss-up race in this year’s general. For the palace intrigue, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton reports that the DCCC is backing Marlene Galán-Woods , a former broadcast journalist who’s never held public office, over former state Rep. Amish Shah , who got the group’s support last cycle. Galán-Woods came in third when she ran in for the same nomination. “She’s on paper a better fit, but you’re dealing with the rather uncomfortable question that she already lost a primary to him,” said a Democratic strategist and DCCC alum. Other Democrats, including Shah himself, are not too pleased. “I think they got it wrong,” Shah told Christa. “I think the Democratic Party voters do not want to see meddling from D.C. here in our district.” From the Hill What’s a week without some House drama? Republican leadership is chugging along with its plan to vote on a rule to advance multiple priorities today: the budget resolution, the National Defense Authorization Act, a short-term continuing resolution to fund federal agencies and a stock-trading ban bill. Speaker Mike Johnson some pushback from members regarding reconciliation 3.0 during a leadership meeting yesterday, sources told NOTUS’ Oriana González, Kadia Goba and Reese Gorman. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), who said he was undecided on the rule, said Republicans need to have more conversations about these bills. But still, Johnson’s confident the rule vote will not blow up: “We’ll pass it. We’re in good shape,” he told NOTUS. Pen to paper: A question hanging over Democrats ahead of November is not just if they can take back control of Congress but what they would do with the power? Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey) is ready to start filling that void today by introducing the MediKids Act, which would basically enroll every child into a section of Medicaid that is already used to provide health services for children from lower-income families, NOTUS’ Paul Kane reports . “ I’m trying to think through everything I can do for the next two-and-a-half years. But I’m also thinking through the next two-and-a-half decades,” Kim, who is just 18 months into his first Senate term, told Paul in an interview. “What do I want to accomplish here, what is the type of senator I want to be? And I think this is, particularly, very meaningful.” From the White House Tariffs are back, baby: Trump slapped 50% tariffs on some Canadian products yesterday, from wine to wood furniture, apparel and cosmetics, NOTUS’ Violet Jira reports . And while Trump threatened to smack America’s northern neighbor for the wildfire smoke that wafted over the border and cost America, by the president’s own math, billions of dollars, a senior administration official said these are “not the so-called wildfire tariffs.” NOTUS PERSPECTIVES “America First” is often associated with bigots and sycophants, argues Matt K. Lewis today at NOTUS Perspectives . But it doesn’t have to be — and he’s reclaiming the phrase. NEW ON NOTUS Switching sides? The Senate Democrats’ albatross, Sen. John Fetterman , is sparking growing speculation that his time on the party rolls is coming to an end. The Pennsylvanian’s embrace of members on the right and his recent declaration that he’d leave the Democratic Party if it officially opposes Israel have left some on edge, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic reports . One Democratic senator, who requested anonymity to speak freely, expressed anxiety over the prospect of an unexpected party switch. “I am concerned,” the senator told NOTUS. title: Senate Republicans Are Now Pushing for More of a Say in Iran War
author: Hamed Ahmadi, Al Weaver, Igor Bobic
summary: Lawmakers worry about escalating war amid troop deaths and rising energy prices.
content: Sen. Bill Cassidy said the latest escalation warrants congressional briefings, individual briefings and “the president speaking to the American people about it, explaining the circumstances,” Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Republican senators are pressing the Trump administration to offer a clearer plan and more information about the Iran war after three U.S. service members were killed and dozens were wounded in renewed attacks in recent days. Several lawmakers said Monday that Congress should no longer remain on the sidelines and that the White House needs to explain where the conflict is headed. “It looked like things were tapering off, and now things look like they’re heating up,” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) told NOTUS. The fighting intensified over the weekend after Iranian attacks killed two U.S. soldiers at a base in Jordan. A third service member was killed in Iraq during the controlled detonation of an Iranian drone. The U.S. military said Monday it was carrying out a 10th consecutive night of strikes against Iran. Trump vowed further retaliation Monday. Cassidy said the latest escalation warrants congressional briefings, individual briefings and “the president speaking to the American people about it, explaining the circumstances,” “I think some sort of authorization of force should be part of that,” Cassidy said, before stopping short of endorsing formally adopting an AUMF. “I just know Congress needs to be involved.” Adding to the troubles is that gas prices are on the rise once again. Prices per gallon eclipsed $4.50 on average in May, but that figure was on the decline until July 4th. Since then, gas prices have sharply increased to nearly $4 per gallon as Iran has again choked off the Strait of Hormuz. “That, to me, is the key consideration in all of this,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters. “That’s going to be key to all these economic questions that have been raised.” No briefing from administration officials appears imminent. Thune told NOTUS that he does not expect a briefing this week. “I don’t know that I expect to,” Thune told NOTUS. “Anytime where we’ve got kinetic activity over there, regular updates are helpful.” Some new information could come tomorrow. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chair of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine will appear before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday, where they are expected to answer questions about the Trump administration’s $87.6 billion supplemental request for Iran war funding. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said Congress should be more involved in approving the war. “I think it’s clear that it is time for Congress to act,” Curtis said. “And that doesn’t mean that it’s necessarily acting, constraining the president, but in fact defining what this looks like.” Curtis said Congress should consider a formal declaration of war on a narrower authorization for specific military action. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said the renewed fighting on July 10 started a new 60-day clock under the War Powers Resolution. “My 60-day clock is ticking.” Tillis said. But not every Republican calling for a clearer plan wants restraint. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) said the administration needs a strategy to break the cycle of Iranian attacks and U.S. retaliation beyond “just hoping for a diplomatic outcome.” “It may very well mean having a plan to militarily resolve this situation,” Rounds said. He that senators should receive classified briefings. Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, echoed Round’s call for a more decisive approach. “I just hope we go ahead and finish the job in Iran,” Wicker said. At issue for members is the timeline. The fighting in Iran kicked off in late February, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle wanting a swift resolution to the war that Trump and administration officials insisted would only go on for a matter of weeks, not months. The “memorandum of understanding” last month brought a temporary halt to activity between the two sides, but has since been brushed aside, leading to the renewed hostilities and worrying lawmakers. “We've lost soldiers. That's a new, very concerning, sad development,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia). “The escalation's concerning.” “You don’t know which way it's going to go,” she . Meanwhile, Democrats plan to force another vote in the Senate this week to cut off hostilities with Iran, aiming to put pressure on vulnerable Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. Last month, four Republican senators broke party lines to support a similar war powers resolution, which was symbolic and not legally binding. “Trump needs to stop this catastrophe and bring our troops home, and Senate Republicans can’t let him off the hook until he does,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said in a floor speech Monday announcing the vote. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) urged Republicans who have concerns about the war to join Democrats in voting for the measure and fulfill their responsibilities as a coequal branch of government. “You can't be against this war and then keep voting to fund the war, and you can't be against this war and keep rejecting these war powers resolutions,” Schatz told NOTUS. Senate Democrats also blocked an effort to begin debate on the annual defense policy bill last week in protest of the Iran war. “Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

title: Trump Is Imposing 50% Tariffs on Goods From Canada
author: Violet Jira
summary: An administration official denied they are “the so-called wildfire tariffs.”
content: The new tariffs, levied via a never-before-used statute, are the largest tariffs the Trump administration has placed on any country since the Supreme Court limited Trump’s tariff authority in February. Saul Loeb/Pool AFP via AP President Donald Trump signed three proclamations Monday that place a 50% tariff on select Canadian goods, which could increase the price of some products imported to the United States from its northern neighbor. The new tariffs, levied via a never-before-used statute, are the largest tariffs the Trump administration has placed on any country since the Supreme Court limited Trump’s tariff authority in February . No United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement exemptions will be honored for the lengthy list of affected goods ranging from wood and wood furniture to apparel and cosmetics. This is a change from last year, when USMCA exemptions partially shielded Canada from the double-digit tariffs placed by Trump on Canada and dozens of other countries. They are set to go into effect in 30 days. The new tariffs come days after Trump threatened Canada with tariffs over wildfire smoke and less than a month after the United States declined to rubber-stamp an extension of the free trade agreement between the United States, Canada and Mexico. A senior administration official told reporters the tariffs are being levied independently of any of these recent events. “These are not the so-called wildfire tariffs. The president has asked for options on that, and options are being shared with him. These tariffs are in response to discriminatory mistreatment by Canada against U.S. products,” the official said in a call with reporters. The administration cited Section of the Tariff Act of , which allows the president to impose tariffs on countries that discriminate against U.S. commerce. A senior administration official told reporters that Canada’s decision to retaliate against tariffs from the U.S. by limiting the sale of American liquor in Canadian government-owned liquor stores and putting quotas on American vehicles and dairy products amounted to discrimination. “These are defensive measures by the United States taken to remedy discriminatory actions by Canada, as the president has made very clear. Both in his campaign and during his administration for the past year and a half, the United States has taken action to protect its national security and to rebalance trade,” the official said. On July 1, the U.S. opted for a series of annual reviews as opposed to extending the USMCA agreement for 16 years as is. The U.S. has engaged in bilateral talks with Mexico but not Canada . The official said the U.S. “remains open to discussions with our Canadian trading partners, especially in the context of the USMCA review.” Over the course of the second Trump administration, the relationship between the U.S. and Canada has continued to devolve, spurred by Trump’s tariffs on Canada and other countries last year. Trump shared a box with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at the World Cup finals on Sunday, a day before announcing the tariffs. “Although the president and the prime minister met and they had a one-on-one, it was not a visit to talk about trade and tariffs from our perspective,” the administration official told reporters.

title: Trump Keeps Claiming Credit for Major Chains’ Summer Price-Cut Promotions
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: First, it was Walmart. Then came grocery chain Giant Eagle. “It's a chicken-and-egg question,” one expert told NOTUS.
content: Walmart says its price cuts went into effect before President Donald Trump announced the decreases came at his administration’s request. Aaron M. Sprecher/AP With no end in sight for the U.S. war with Iran and President Donald Trump threatening new tariffs for everything from wildfire smoke to oil sales , American consumers are feeling the squeeze of higher prices at the pump and the check-out line. As a result, the president has taken to publicly calling for companies to lower their prices as a show of patriotism and even support for his agenda — pressure that he has suggested in recent weeks is working. First, it was Walmart. Then came grocery chain Giant Eagle this weekend, which Trump said was “stepping up in a big and bold way to answer my call” to lower prices via a summer promotional sale. “Other Grocery Chains must immediately follow the lead of these absolute Patriots at Giant Eagle and Walmart,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. But it’s not clear the president had anything to do with these discounts. Ricky Volpe, an agribusiness professor at California Polytechnic State University, said he expects promotional activity to be “red hot right now” as food-price inflation accelerates. “I will just say, from the outset, it is absolutely not clear if the actions of Walmart or Giant Eagle are a result of [Trump]. It's a chicken-and-egg question because summer promotions are very common,” Volpe told NOTUS. This was especially true for Walmart’s summer promotion, a source close to the company told NOTUS. Walmart’s lower summer prices went into effect a week before Trump declared that the company had launched the savings event “at my Administration's request.” “The timing there I think is just important to note, because the pricing went into effect before anything else had happened,” the source said. When asked directly if Giant Eagle launched its summer “On Sale This Season” promotion in response to or in conjunction with the Trump administration, the supermarket chain did not directly answer. “We are aware of the President’s message in support of the On Sale This Season pricing initiative Giant Eagle launched on July 9,” the company wrote in an emailed statement. “We look forward to this program helping our customers save all summer long.” When asked whether the administration had any communication with the supermarket chains, spokesperson Kush Desai said: “The Trump Administration stays in close contact with retailers to ensure savings are getting passed on to American consumers, and results like this prove the strategy is working.” A more compelling explanation for the sweeping summer sale at Giant Eagle is Kroger’s ongoing effort to acquire the grocery chain in a $1.65 billion deal, Volpe said. “Giant Eagle announcing these massive price rollbacks, I would gather, is more likely related to this pending acquisition that's making a lot of headlines in an attempt to assuage concerns,” Volpe said. There is “no real sense of seasonality or cyclicality to food prices in general,” according to Volpe, and there are a multitude of reasons why a retailer might decide to lower prices, including competing with other chains and driving traffic to certain stores. Linking promotional activity to any presidential administration creates a “slippery slope for these retailers,” Volpe . “I really, really doubt that any retailer of any stripe wants to credit the Trump administration for the lower prices, and that's not a political statement,” Volpe said. “It's because linking their behavior to pressure from the president sets a worrisome precedent for these retailers.” Walmart and its subsidiary Sam’s Club lowered the price of in its recent savings campaign — which is one of Trump’s continued policy goals . Walmart and Sam’s Club also lowered prices on various items to honor the anniversary of the nation’s founding, according to Trump. “Walmart will, in particular, be dropping the price for a pound of ground by almost 15%, among many other products,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This is a huge deal for the many millions of Americans who, smartly, shop at Walmart, which is a truly patriotic Company who loves the U.S.A.” Giant Eagle also lowered its prices, as well as roughly other items. The grocery chain launched its summer version of the On Sale This Season, after the “company saw a strong customer response to its fall” version of the pricing effort, according to Giant Eagle’s press release , which made no mention of the president. The Consumer Price Index for all items increased 3.5% in June year over year, though prices dipped .4% in the month of June as a temporary pause in the Iran war slowed fuel prices. Americans, though, still think groceries are too expensive. In a Washington Post-Ipsos poll conducted from July 8 to July 13, 66% of Americans said they would describe the cost of groceries as unaffordable — a notable increase from the 45% who answered that way in February before the war. Americans are also concerned about broader economic woes. Ninety-five percent of U.S. adults believe the country is suffering an affordability crisis, according to a survey taken by the Harris Poll for The Guardian in May and June . Trump has previously called affordability a “hoax” and a “Democrat scam.”

title: Air Force One-Maxxing
author: Brett Bachman, Manuela Silva
content: The presidential limousine, with President Donald Trump inside, arrives in front of the new Air Force One, Wednesday, July 1, , at Joint Base Andrews, Md. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 20, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST President Donald Trump insists that his new, Qatari-donated Air Force One has all of the necessary security features — but he’s still taking it out of service for at least a month to be “maxed out,” he told a reporter . His administration is seeking the phone records of journalists who reported on the jet’s security shortcomings. One reporter’s mother was even targeted as part of the investigation, according to The New York Times . Trump is claiming credit for a summer promotional sale the grocery chain Giant Eagle is running for staple food items. It’s not clear that Trump played any role in the company’s decision to run the sale, which it said was an extension of the chain’s successful fall discount campaign. THE HILL Lindsey Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), told Fox News that she will run for a full term after being nominated as his interim replacement. Rep. Russell Fry (R-South Carolina) also declared his candidacy, but a victory could leave his House seat vacant for months at a time when the GOP majority is razor thin. THE ADMINISTRATION The Houthis are imposing a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, which could drastically cut Saudi oil exports just as the global oil supply was beginning to rebound . The Pentagon identified the two soldiers killed in Jordan after Iran launched missiles at a U.S. military base. Taylor Farms said the Food and Drug Administration had “apologized” for a false-positive test result linking its iceberg lettuce to the ongoing cyclosporiasis outbreak. The FDA said it did no such thing, and that despite the faulty test, its investigation still points toward the produce giant as the likely source of the outbreak. A man is in custody after allegedly setting off fireworks and lighting a blaze outside a federal building in Manhattan that houses ICE and FBI offices. The Department of Homeland Security described the alleged perpetrator as an “anti-ICE rioter” and said it was investigating the incident as a potential act of terrorism. ACROSS THE POND “King of the North” Andy Burnham took over for Keir Starmer as the United Kingdom’s new prime minister today after meeting with King Charles III . ‘HERITAGE FOUNDATION VANCE’ WAS ALREADY TAKEN Thank you for reading! title: Trump Taking Qatari-Donated AF1 Out of Service to Be ‘Maxed Out’
author: Brett Bachman
summary: The jet’s security has become a matter of contention in recent weeks.
content: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin President Donald Trump’s new, Qatari-donated Air Force One is set to be taken out of service for at least a month to be “maxed out,” he said on Sunday when asked about concerns over the jet’s security measures. He rode on the $ million jet from New Jersey, where he attended the World Cup final, to Washington Sunday evening and addressed reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. “It has a lot of capability, but as I understand it, in about a month or so, they’re going to send it to have it be maxed out,” Trump said, adding: “It’ll take about a month.” It remains unclear what upgrades Trump was referring to. jet’s security has become a matter of contention in recent weeks. The Trump administration subpoenaed several journalists with The New York Times after the newspaper reported on security concerns with the 14-year-old plane, which was given to him by the government of Qatar last year. The Times subsequently filed a motion to quash the subpoenas, while vowing to fight the administration’s efforts to interfere with its reporting. “They violate the constitutional rights of The Times and its journalists,” David McCraw, a lawyer for the Times, wrote in a statement last week. “We are going to court to defend our journalists’ rights to report freely on the administration and to provide the public with stories that matter.” Trump took the plane on its maiden voyage to Turkey for a NATO summit earlier this month, but scuttled his plans to return on the jet, which was instead sent to the United States’ Mildenhall Air Force Base in England to be toured by soldiers. The president wrote on social media that he was taking the older aircraft “for old times’ sake” and he repeatedly denied that the switch was made due to security concerns. “The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the president and his staff,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said at the time. “As the president has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal — including distraction and misdirection — to address those threats,” he .

title: War's Mounting Toll
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva, Jenna Monnin
content: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Today’s notice: The U.S. death toll rises in the Iran war. Maine’s Troy Jackson heads to the Democratic nomination. The U.S. Senate’s focus isn’t legislation. And: How Republicans are campaigning on the housing bill Trump called a “big yawn.” THE LATEST Three U.S. service members engaged in the Iran war were killed in action in two separate incidents over the weekend, and U.S. Central Command is trying to verify whether remains discovered near the site of one attack, in Jordan , match a fourth service member who was considered missing. A total of 17 U.S. service members have died and dozens have been injured since the start of the war. As the escalation continues — last night marked nine consecutive days of U.S. strikes on Iran — it remains unclear how the rise in the death toll may sway public sentiment and congressional support. Most Americans already disapprove of the war. Top congressional leaders offered their condolences , but delivered mixed messages on what should happen with the ongoing war. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) said President Donald Trump “is right to unleash hell on [the service members’] killers” while Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called for de‑escalation. “No more American heroes need to die because of this reckless war of choice,” Jeffries said on X . Trump, on his way back to the White House from attending the World Cup final in New Jersey, said the U.S. strikes against Iran on Sunday night would be in honor of those fallen service members. “We feel very badly but you know those great people, those great patriots were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. “We hit them very hard again tonight.” Open tabs: Federal Agents Were Told F.B.I. Will No Longer Investigate ICE Confrontations (NYT); Trump immigration officials seek to mend frayed ties with business as arrests spike (WaPo); Trump praises Burnham over plans to fast-track North Sea oil (Telegraph); Russia pounds Kyiv in major ballistic missile attack (Reuters); 'Happy and healthy': JD and Usha Vance welcome fourth child (USA Today) From the campaign trail The Democratic field in Maine dramatically thinned out over the weekend, as Troy Jackson effectively clinched the nomination for U.S. Senate. As counties chose their delegates for this Saturday’s official nominating convention, more than half of those selected said they backed Jackson, Jenna reports . Before Jackson became the presumptive nominee, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she was exiting the race to focus on her role as the state’s chief election officer amid Trump’s attacks on ballot integrity. Later Sunday, former state CDC Director Nirav Shah and former Capitol Hill staffer Jordan Wood also dropped out and immediately endorsed Jackson. Shah said he stepped aside because “the Democratic Party must be unified” to beat Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). Advice for Republicans campaigning on the big housing bill: “You could talk about the policy. You don't have to talk about how it became law,” a GOP strategist told NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández . Raymond dives into the emerging awkward situation for purple-district Republicans: They have a big, bipartisan bill on a topic Americans care about, but the head of their party called it a “big yawn” and refused to sign it. “I don’t speak for the president,” Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R- Pennsylvania) told Raymond. “I know my voters, my constituents. My electors are super excited about the package.” From the Hill How the Senate stopped being the Senate, in charts. The numbers don’t lie: Nomination confirmations made up less than 20% of total roll-call votes prior to — the year then-Majority Leader Harry Reid nuked the filibuster for most nominations. By the end of , nominations topped 60% of roll-call votes. NOTUS’ Avani Kalra crunched the numbers on how the World’s Greatest Deliberative Body has morphed into the world’s additional arena for partisan squabbles. The bottom line: More and more legislation is done through party-line reconciliation votes, and more and more floor time is devoted to confirmations. NOTUS METRO Sign up for our local newsletter. NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for all the latest , launching today! Local news. Will Free Buses Ever Arrive in D.C.? By Zara Norman Sports desk. Josiah Gray Still Wants to Help the Nats. Maybe Even This Year. By Jesse Dougherty NOTUS PERSPECTIVES Is Pennsylvania governor (and likely Democratic presidential candidate) Josh Shapiro actually good at governing? At NOTUS Perspectives, two local reporters chronicle his setbacks in Pennsylvania . Plus: The Reflecting Pool may have turned green, and the state fair may have been a dud, but Trump’s Garden of American Heroes is a great idea , argues Ben Jacobs. NEW ON NOTUS Clocking the daylight saving time effort in the Senate. “It’s got a lot of opposition,” Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS’ Al Weaver . Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) has pledged to stand in the way of this idea for as long as time itself. That’s a stark outlook compared to the House. Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tennessee) played the Beatles’ “Here Comes the Sun” as he presided over the floor during the chamber’s vote to make daylight saving time permanent last week. The bill passed - . But the cynicism in the House is palpable when it comes to the Senate. Members have seen their colleagues on the other side of the Capitol squash too many of their legislative dreams to predict when Americans won’t have to change their clocks twice a year. “They’ve all gone to the Sizzler for the early-bird special. They wanted to get to the fondue bar. So I don't know,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee) told Manuela of when a bill could pass. Now It’s a $37 Billion Problem.
